newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-High St spending, housing to boost UK GDP.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-High St spending, housing to boost UK GDP.

text.p: Britain's economy grew a little faster in the third quarter, bolstered by robust consumer spending and a revived housing market, analysts said.
A Reuter poll of economists found a consensus expecting 0.7 percent GDP growth on the quarter and 2.3 percent year-on-year.
In the second quarter, the economy grew by 0.5 percent and 2.2 percent year-on-year.
"We look for GDP growth of 0.7 percent, marking a move to an above-trend pace," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Constraints on third quarter growth will come from weaker energy and mining output and a moderate fall in oil production.

But free-spending consumers and increased housing starts, prompted by rising property prices, will balance that. "Although industrial production is likely to show only a modest rise in Q3 due to weaker energy and mining output, the consumer-led recovery should boost service sector output," Barr said.
The figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Friday.

Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, also backed the consensus forecast. But he said the recent high rate of growth in the service sector may have eased slightly in line with slower growth in retail sales in the third quarter.
Although high street activity is on the increase, it grew at a slightly slower rate in the third quarter than in the second.

However, he agreed a strong housing market would have a positive effect. "Housing market activity has continued to strengthen but retail sales have almost certainly slowed compared to the 1.3 percent expansion seen in Q2."

September retail sales data, released on Wednesday, showed sales for the third quarter were 0.8 percent up on the second. But in the second quarter, they were 1.3 percent higher than in Q1. Housing starts rose seven percent in three months to August.

The GDP figures assume more importance than usual, being the last key pieces of economic data released before the monthly monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George on October 30. "The figures will be closely watched to determine whether the recent pick-up in consumer activity has been mirrored by the overall economy," Loynes said.
"Strong growth would almost certainly prompt Eddie George into stepping up his campaign for higher interest rates."
Minutes from two recent monetary meetings showed George would prefer base rates to be at six percent, not 5.75.
Economists at UBS forecast 0.8 percent GDP growth in the third quarter, just above the consensus.
They said manufacturing activity would have picked up a little while the strength of consumer demand would have sustained service sector growth.
"The service sector momentum seen over the past year is expected to have been maintained by the strength of consumer demand, clearly evident in recent retail sales data," they said.

Although September's sales data showed slower quarterly growth, sales over the three month period were 3.4 percent up on the same period a year ago, the highest growth rate since December 1994, the Office for National Statistics said.
"The three-month trend shows things have really picked up," Barr said.

The UBS analysts said energy production probably fell in Q3 but said agricultural output would have reversed second quarter weakness related to fears over BSE, or "mad cow" disease. "And a property market revival bodes well for output of the construction sector," they said.
